faq.q: What is the difference between rumination and reflection?
faq.a: Rumination is passive, repetitive focus on your negative feelings and their causes that goes nowhere and tends to worsen mood. Reflection covers the same material on purpose and moves toward understanding or a next step. In Treynor and colleagues' 2003 analysis, brooding predicted more depressive symptoms a year later, while reflection predicted fewer.

faq.q: Is it bad to ask yourself why you feel this way?
faq.a: It depends on where you stand. Watkins found that abstract, evaluative 'why' thinking about a failure kept people's mood lower, but Kross, Ayduk and Mischel (2005) found that asking why from a self-distanced perspective reduced anger. Ask 'how' when you're close to the event and save 'why' for after you've stepped back.

faq.q: How do you stop ruminating at night?
faq.a: Write the event down in a few sentences using your own name instead of 'I', ask what you'd tell a friend in the same spot, then turn to concrete 'how' questions and end with one small step or a set time tomorrow to think about it. If night-time loops are frequent or come with low mood, talk to a doctor or therapist.

It can. Lyubomirsky and colleagues (2006) found that writing or talking about a bad experience improved well-being and health four weeks later compared with thinking about it privately, and Park, Ayduk and Kross (2016) found expressive writing increased self-distancing. The effects are modest, and analyzing happy memories in writing seemed to backfire.

Self-distancing means thinking about your own experience from a step back, as an observer would. Ways to do it include picturing the scene from across the room, using your name or 'you' instead of 'I', asking what you'd tell a friend, and imagining how the event will look years from now.

informationGain: It resolves the apparent conflict between Watkins's finding that 'why' questions fuel rumination and Kross's finding that 'why' from a distance helps, turning it into one usable rule (ask how when close, why only after stepping back) with a step-by-step method built on it.
